placement.position_note: PARTY-LINE FRONTAGE, DERIVED FROM THE COMMITTED PLAT (T-0078). This building does not stand centred on a lot at a typology setback: it stands ON the south face of blk_randolph_market, the block's Washington Street frontage, whose line and bearing are read from the block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json — the same committed geometry the lot grid and the corridor gate are derived from. Its front wall is 1.50 m back from that lot line, which is the closest line the plat module's own margin allows and is not a measurement of this frontage, and its west wall is fixed by the east wall of recon_1835_blk_randolph_market_d1_10, which it shares a party line with. The bearing is the face's own, so the front looks square at Washington Street. The run carries no lateral offset, because a shared party wall is one wall and cannot wander. WHAT IS INVENTED IS STILL EVERYTHING THAT MATTERS: that a building stood here at all, which building it was, and that these particular units stood shoulder to shoulder. What the 1834 South Water Street view supports is the TREATMENT — a continuous working row of party walls rather than detached cottages set back on grass. The treatment is what this placement takes from it, and a run standing on any other face of the town is borrowing it from that one street: the view draws a row, it does not place this row. Standing on a derived block face is not standing on a recovered lot, and the side lot lines this row crosses were always conjectural.

persons.name: J. Garland
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED MAN ON A RECONSTRUCTED ROOF. The papers name him and this household's dwelling does not: what is attested is the person and his trade, and what remains the reconstruction's is everything about where he lived. He is printed as 'J. GARLAND' and the corpus reads his trade as cooper. Cited at the Democrat of 11 June 1834, column 11. THIS ROOF DID NOT COME FROM HIS RECORD. The household was raised by the occupation census because the town of 3,265 people in 398 dwellings needed a cooper and no documented one was available; the register (data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json, action `replace_invented`) is what says one now is. The dwelling's existence, position and footprint are unchanged and still conjectural, and nothing here claims he slept in it — only that the town's need for this trade is met by a man the papers name rather than by one this project invented. The invented name this record used to carry, and its name_basis block, are retired: an invented name is not kept beside a documented one. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1); the placement is L205. He is placed nowhere in particular by his own record, which is the condition of taking ANY roof of his trade — a man the papers put on a named street takes only a roof the plat stands on that street (T-0367), and one they place somewhere this scene cannot honour is refused outright. READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry.

residents.research_note: RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD - fourth of 4 cooper households in this layer, in the north division. A TOWN PACKING THOUSANDS OF HOGS A SEASON NEEDS COOPERS, AND THIS DATASET HELD NONE. Andreas records that Clybourne packed some 250 head of cattle and about 2,000 hogs in the season of 1833, that George W. Dole packed a further 250 cattle and 1,000 hogs at the same place, and that the Newberry & Dole house on the South Branch packed 300 cattle and 1,400 hogs in 1834 (scan p. 1151). Packed provisions travel in barrels and barrels are made by coopers. The documented layer holds a packer, two slaughter-houses and not one cooper. Four cooper households are inferred against the schedule's six W3 cooper, wagon or wheelwright shops. METHOD: the count comes from the occupation census in data/reconstruction/1835_inferred_household_programme.json, which calibrates every trade against three things this project already holds - the 1835 town census (3,265 people, 398 dwellings), Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 (about fifty named people, most with a trade, in a settlement of some 350), and the reconstruction specification's roof schedule, whose workshop and store family targets are treated as the ceiling on a trade rather than as its measure. Every count is stated NET of the documented layer: this dataset infers a tradesman only where it cannot name one. RETIRED AN INVENTED NAME (T-0264). This household was raised by the occupation census and named from the invented-name pools. The newspaper register matched it to J. Garland, a documented cooper the corpus names 1 time(s) and places nowhere in particular, and he now holds the roof. What changed is WHO: the argument for the household, its dwelling and its position are untouched and still the reconstruction's, and the person's grade is `inferred` — a real man with reconstructed details — rather than `attested`, which would claim the dwelling too. tools/replace_invented_residents.py derives this deal and prints every candidate it refused. T-0489: reconstructed occupancy retired; evidence-based person retained and unplaced.

what_it_supplies: that a named trade was being carried on in Chicago in a named week, and often where
self-reported addresses, which are the strongest address evidence this project has: the advertiser was paying, and his customers had to find him
dissolution, removal and replacement notices — the only thing that keeps a documented business out of the 1835 town under the owner's ruling 3
post-office letter lists, naming residents by the hundred (ruling 1: a listed name mints a resident candidate, flagged letter_list_only)
the village and later town ordinances, printed complete — the 7 November 1833 code is the richest single item in the run
arrivals and clearances, which date the piers and the harbour as working structures
public notices that fix a building as a polling place, an auction site or a meeting place on a given day
the paper's own imprint, self-reported: the corner of South Water and Clark streets
twenty-one months of continuous weekly attestation ending three weeks before the scene date, including the issue printed on 1835-07-01

the specific corner of any junction it names: 'on the corner of' does not say which of the four
anything at all from an engraving — see trap 1; the cuts are the printer's stock
proof that a business named in 1833 or 1834 still stood on 1835-07-01; that is ruling 3's survival liberty, and it is a liberty
an argument from silence, unless corpus.json shows the issues either side of the silence are both in the deposit
a reading that outranks a scan read of the same passage — see ruling 2 and the C. & I. HARMON case

frontage.why: T-0317, the successor T-0028's programme owes, and the first parcel in this project where the core density standard's corner clause and the end rule point in OPPOSITE directions. THE FACE IS MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED, by the command T-A14 made of it — tools/measure_street_frontage.py randolph washington market franklin — and on the committed dataset Randolph carries 7 documented records and 7 inferred households against Washington's 1 and 0, Market's 2 and 1, and Franklin's 2 and 1. Randolph is this block's business face by the town's own record and it is FULL: the first deal took lots 0 and 2 and the inferred-household layer's two sawyer dwellings hold 4 and 6, so every lot on that face carries a roof and the two lots this block has left are both on the Washington tier. WHAT BINDS IS THE STANDARD'S THIRD CLAUSE. Lot 1 is the block's one free CORNER lot, the south-west one, fronting Washington along its long edge and Market Street along its short one, and a corner lot BUILDS TO THE CORNER — an east-anchored run packs back toward the middle of the face and stops wherever its roofs run out, so the corner is the one piece of frontage a row can never reach. The run is packed WEST to it. AND THE GRADING RUNS THE OTHER WAY, which is the finding here. On blk_randolph_dearborn's third deal the free corner was at Dearborn — the only crossing of the main stem in July 1835 — so building to the corner and standing the best roof nearest the crossing were the same act, and the parcel could not tell the two clauses apart. This corner is at MARKET, the far end of the face from that bridge, so they separate: the corner clause fixes WHERE THE ROW STANDS and the end rule fixes WHICH ROOF STANDS WHERE IN IT, and on this block they are demonstrably different questions. THE END RULE IS READ, NOT ASSERTED: tools/measure_end_rule.py reads this face at a spread of 71.03 m and a unit step of 6.07 m under the walked criterion and grades on it, while the same face under T-A11's straight line reads 4.82 m and is BELOW THE FLOOR — so the walk is what makes a grading possible here at all, and the straight line would have been grading this parcel's own declared setback invention. The row is therefore graded EAST, toward Franklin and the bridge beyond it: the meanest dwelling stands on the corner and the best closes the run at the east end. NO COORDINATE IS AUTHORED: the line, its bearing, the lot's own stretch of it and the end the run packs toward are all read from the committed block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json, and the 1.5 m setback is the plat module's own lot margin rather than a measurement of this frontage. The Washington face carries no committed street wall for the run to adopt — the two roofs already standing on that tier are one-per-lot placements set back inside their own lots — so this run is the first line on the face and states the margin rather than adopting one.
